claims.text: The tensile-creep, hardness, and elastic-modulus behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by thermally induced differential expansion within an initially homogeneous microstructure.
Thermal exposure causes local compositional variations, incipient phase segregation, or precipitation in HfNbTaTiZr.
The emerging heterogeneous regions have different thermal-expansion coefficients.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between heterogeneous regions generates internal residual stresses.
The mismatch-induced residual stresses alter dislocation mobility.
The starting as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase and nominally homogeneous.
Annealing at 600–800 °C and exposure up to 1250 °C can be used to test the proposed thermal-mismatch mechanism.
External constraint or thermal gradients accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch relative to uniform, unconstrained cooling.
Differentially expanding regions produce internal thermal stresses that impede or otherwise modify dislocation motion.
Mismatch-induced internal stresses alter high-temperature creep behavior.
Mismatch-induced internal stresses produce the hardening observed after aging or cold rolling.
Mismatch-induced internal stresses shift the alloy's elastic moduli over the studied temperature range.
Samples subjected to conditions that accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch will have greater creep resistance at 1250 °C than freely expanding, uniformly cooled samples.
Samples subjected to conditions that accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch will have higher microhardness after cold rolling than baseline samples.
Samples subjected to conditions that accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch will show a more pronounced temperature dependence of elastic modulus than baseline samples.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply from room temperature to 1250 °C under cold rolling, aging at 600–800 °C, and tensile-creep testing conditions.
Chemical ordering or major phase transformations could dominate outside the stated conditions and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
TEM and XRD can test whether the compared processing routes produce different amounts of segregation or precipitation.
A lack of statistically significant differences in creep, hardness, or elastic modulus between mismatch-suppressed and baseline samples would falsify the governing-mechanism hypothesis.
A lack of any difference in heterogeneity or precipitate formation between the compared groups would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Constraint is described inconsistently: it is proposed as a way to either enhance or suppress mismatch, the prediction treats imposed constraint as accentuating mismatch, while the falsification design treats matrix embedding and constrained expansion as suppressing internal stress. Thus, the causal direction of the central intervention is not consistently defined.

The design proposes embedding the sample in a matrix with a closely matched thermal-expansion coefficient to suppress internal stress, but matching the matrix to the bulk alloy does not necessarily suppress stresses caused by differential expansion among internal heterogeneous regions. The designated comparison may therefore fail to isolate the stated mediator.
